reasons: Anchor read: Russian 'Что ни день, ни ночь покою нет' (love-sickness). Partner AM 519a 4to 24v:34 is Alexanders saga, a 13th-c. translation of Walter of Châtillon's Latin Alexandreis: the army may not rest at night any more than by day (military march). Etymology fine: hvíld (*hwīl-, Kroonen s.v. *hwīlō- < *kʷih1-l-, citing OCS pokoi < *kʷoih1-o-) ~ pokoj, nótt ~ ночь. But 'neither day nor night rest' is a universal merism, contexts differ (emotional vs march), and the Norse witness is translated from Latin: derivative and generic.
derivative_risk: high (Alexanders saga is a translation of the Latin Alexandreis)
known: no specific literature; day-and-night merism is cross-linguistically common

reasons: Anchor: Jómsvíkinga saga 'lét sveininn vatni ausa og nafn gefa' (naming a newborn). Partner PlCasin 30 'comoediai nomen dare uobis uolo' = announcing a play's title to the audience. Only nafn ~ nomen is cognate (*h1nómn̥); gefa and dare are not cognate; 'give a name' is a cross-linguistically trivial construction and the situations are unrelated. Latin 'nomen dare' and Christian baptismal usage also make the Norse phrase non-diagnostic.
known: the inherited formula is *h1nómn̥ dʰeh1- 'put a name' (Hitt., Ved., Gk., Arm.), widely discussed; 'give a name' is not it

reasons: Anchor verified: Norse law 'ef þat kømr lífi í ljós ok verðr skírt' (child born alive into the light and baptized). Lucretius 1.22, 1.179, 2.617, 5.224-225 'in luminis oras' all checked: coming into/brought into the shores of light = birth/coming into being (5.224 explicitly from the mother's womb). Il. 16.188, 19.118 Eileithyia 'ἐξάγαγε πρὸ φόως' (birth) checked. ljós (*leuhsa-, s-stem of *leuk-) and lūmen (*leuk-s-men-) are root cognates (Kroonen cites Lat. lūmen); Greek renews with φάος. Congruent birth context and 'into light' directional frame, but: only one cognate element (the noun, and a different derivative), the verb differs, 'come into the light = be born' is a natural metaphor found widely, and the Norse legal phrase may reflect Latin/Christian 'in lucem venire/edere' (baptism follows in the same clause).
derivative_risk: medium (Christian/Latin legal phrasing; Lucretian phrase is Ennian)
known: 'see the light (of the sun)' = live (Gk ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο, Ved. sū́ryaṃ dṛś-) is a known inherited figure; birth as 'coming into the light' is related and discussed for Greek/Latin

reasons: Grágás s290 verified: cover the corpse 'svo að hvortki eti dýr né fuglar'. Il. 18.271, 22.42 verified: 'κύνες καὶ γῦπες ἔδονται/ἔδοιεν'. Only the verb is cognate (*h1ed-), and 'eat' is the basic verb any language would use; the subject nouns are generic categories (beasts, birds) not cognate with dogs/vultures; Greek is a curse/threat of non-burial, Norse a burial-law prescription. Scavenging of corpses by beasts and birds is an ordinary reality; no collocational evidence beyond the inevitable verb.
known: the 'corpse as prey for dogs and birds' motif is discussed for Homer and Near Eastern/Germanic battle poetry (beasts of battle); typological/areal

reasons: Anchor (Þiðreks saga, HolmPerg 4 fol) verified: 'mærkr af rau-do gulli' as a gift. Theognis 450 'χρυσόν ἐρυθρὸν' (gold tested on the touchstone) verified; Il. 9.365 verified but there ἐρυθρόν qualifies χαλκόν, not gold, so it is not a 'red gold' witness. rauðr ~ ἐρυθρός (*h1rewdʰ-/*h1rudʰ-ro-) correct; gold renewed (χρυσός a Semitic loan). Germanic 'red gold' is a strong formula, but Greek has one isolated instance in a purity simile; the colour of pure gold is a natural description, and Þiðreks saga derives from Low German material. One cognate element, high generic risk.
derivative_risk: medium (Þiðreks saga from Low German sources; Germanic-internal)
known: Germanic 'red gold' (OE read gold, ON rautt gull, OHG rōtaz gold) is well known; also OIr. dergór (non-cognate adjective)

reasons: Árna saga biskups s820 (w3/3) verified: 'undir fótum troðið frelsi kirkjunnar' (church's liberty trampled underfoot). Lucretius 1.78-79 'religio pedibus subiecta ... opteritur' verified. fótum ~ pedibus cognate (*pṓd-) but 'trample underfoot' is a universal metaphor and the Norse is clerical prose in a Latin ecclesiastical register (Vulgate 'sub pedibus conculcare', Ps. 90/91:13, Mt 7:6 etc.). Derivative and generic.

Vuk 1598:73 verified: 'Црна земља испуца од суше' (black earth cracked with drought). Pindar O. 9.50 'χθόνα ... μέλαιναν' (flood) verified. земља (*zemja < *dʰǵʰem-) ~ χθών (*dʰéǵʰōm) cognate; adjective renewed (crn vs μέλας). 'Black earth' is a genuine and well-attested epithet (Homeric γαῖα μέλαινα, Slavic 'crna zemlja'), but only the noun is cognate, soil colour makes the epithet natural, and the partner contexts are opposite catastrophes. Defensible but not compelling.
known: 'dark/black earth' is discussed as inherited: Hitt. dankui- tēkan ~ Gk γαῖα/χθὼν μέλαινα (tēkan ~ χθών cognate); Slavic 'crna/syra zemlja' often cited

reasons: Norse law MLB 76r:1 verified: offence 'með orðum eða verkum' in the Christmas peace. Il. 1.504 'ἢ ἔπει ἢ ἔργῳ' and Il. 11.703 'ἐπέων ... ἔργων' verified. verk ~ ἔργον cognate (*werǵ-); orð (*wurda- < *h2u(o)rdʰ-o-, Kroonen; cognate with Lat. verbum) vs ἔπος (*wekʷ-) not cognate. The word/deed merism is genuinely old and widespread, but in a medieval Christian law the formula is fully explained by Latin/Christian 'verbo et opere / dictis factisve' legal and biblical usage (Col. 3:17, 1 Jn 3:18). One cognate element, high derivative risk.
known: 'word and deed' merism is discussed in IE phraseology (Gk ἔπος/ἔργον, Av. vacah-/šyaoθna-); widely noted as areal and Christian too

reasons: Bylina ruws 390731:332 verified: 'чашу меду сладкаго' served at a feast. Od. 10.184, 9.162 'μέθυ ἡδύ' at feasting verified. мёд ~ μέθυ (*médʰu) cognate; сладкий (*soldъ-) not cognate with ἡδύς (*sweh2dú-), so the epithet is a renewal. Congruent feast context, but honey/mead is inherently sweet; the epithet is generic in Russian. The inherited formula proper is Gk μέθυ ἡδύ ~ Ved. svādú mádhu (cognate both members), which the Russian does not preserve.
known: 'sweet mead' *swādú médʰu (Gk μέθυ ἡδύ, Ved. mádhu svādú/svādór mádhvaḥ) is a known inherited collocation; the Slavic renewal is not

reasons: Anchor HolmPerg-4-fol 'rau-do gulli' verified; partner bylina line 27287 'Красно золото не ржавеет' (Dobrynja bylina; 27284 also 'красна золота') verified. Only gold is cognate (*ǵʰelh3-/*ǵʰl̥h3-tó-), and that is merely the referent; красный is not cognate with rauðr and in Russian folk epic means 'beautiful/fine' as a stock epithet (красна девица, красно солнышко), so 'red' semantics are doubtful. No phraseological evidence beyond naming gold.
known: Germanic 'red gold' known; Russian красно золото is a Slavic stock epithet

reasons: Vuk 1658:315-316 verified ('док је Цера и Видојевице и на небу сунца и мјесеца', duration of a battlefield's fame); Vuk 21690:174-175 and 10111:178 'доклен тече сунца и мјесеца' verified. AVŚ 6.75.6 'śaśvatībhyaḥ samābhyaḥ yāvat sūryaḥ asat divi' and AVP 19.15.16 'yāvat sūryo asad divi' verified (temporal). AVP 19.9.19 'yāvad dyaur yāvat pṛthivī yāvad ābhāti sūryaḥ' verified but it is spatial extent ('as far as'), introducing a poison spell, not an eternity formula: misused. Hdt 8.143.2 verified ('as long as the sun goes the same road ... never'). Sun words cognate (*seh2ul-/*sh2un-); 'in the sky' locative is a near match (небу vs diví, renewed). But 'as long as sun (and moon) endure' is a near-universal and Near Eastern eternity formula; Serbian 'sun and moon' matches Ps. 72(71):5 in the Church Slavonic Psalter. Areal/typological; derivative risk for Serbian.
derivative_risk: medium (Psalter Ps. 72:5 'with the sun and moon'; Near Eastern oath formulae)
known: eternity-by-sun formula is widely noted (Near Eastern, Biblical, Greek oaths); areal

reasons: Víglundar saga s1272 verified: 'leggur höfuð sitt í kné honum og biður hann gera af slíkt er hann vill' (submission). Il. 1.500-501 Thetis 'λάβε γούνων ... ὑπ᾽ ἀνθερεῶνος' verified; PlCurc 630 'per tua genua te opsecro' verified. kné ~ γόνυ ~ genu (*ǵónu-) correct. Knees as locus of supplication/submission is a real shared figure, but the gestures differ (laying one's head on the knees vs grasping knees/swearing by them), the verbs are not cognate, the Norse saga is late (c. 1400), and knee-supplication is a widespread human posture (Near East too).
known: knee-grasping supplication and 'knees' as seat of power/fate are well discussed (Onians, Gould 1973 on hiketeia); Norse head-on-knee submission gesture known from sagas

reasons: Same anchor as L003 (verified). LucrDRN1 1.170 'oras in luminis exit', 2.617 'uiuam progeniem ... in oras luminis edant', 5.224-225 '... in luminis oras nixibus ex aluo matris natura profudit' verified; these are birth/coming-into-being, closest at 5.224-225. ljós ~ lūmen root cognates (*leuk-), predicates not cognate. Natural metaphor, single cognate element, and possible Latin/Christian legal source for the Norse inheritance rule. Duplicate of L003.

Vuk 47821:18 'грло, бјеље од снијега' and Il. 10.437 'λευκότεροι χιόνος' verified. Etymology wrong: снијег continues *sneigʷʰ- but χιών continues *ǵʰyōm (Arm. jiwn, Lat. hiems, Ved. himá-; Beekes s.v. χιών); the Greek *sneigʷʰ- reflex is νίφα. No cognate pair at all; 'whiter than snow' is a universal (and Biblical, Ps. 51:7) comparison.

Egill's verse (Wolf-Aug-9-10-4to 51v:19 w1/2) verified: 'hǫfum oft roðit brandi ... rjóðum sverð í blóði'. Il. 10.484 and 21.21 'ἄορι θεινομένων ἐρυθαίνετο δ᾽ αἵματι γαῖα/ὕδωρ' verified. rjóða (*h1reudʰ-) and ἐρυθαίνω (denominative to ἐρυθρός) share the root; blood and sword words not cognate. The Greek reddens ground/water passively, the Norse actively reddens the weapon (a skaldic commonplace). 'Red(den) with blood' is a universal image; one root shared, different syntax and object.
known: 'redden (weapon) in blood' is a known skaldic commonplace; no IE comparison known to me
dictionaries_checked: kroonen-pgmc s.v. *reudan- (equates ON rjóða with Gk ἐρεύθω)

reasons: Anchor 'nafn gefa' verified. Od. 19.403 'ὄνομ᾽ ... θῆαι', 19.406 'τίθεσθ᾽ ὄνομ᾽' (naming the newborn Odysseus) and Od. 18.5 'ὄνομ᾽ ... θέτο πότνια μήτηρ' verified: genuine *h1nómn̥ + *dʰeh1- naming formula. RV 1.103.4d 'nā́ma dadhé' verified but means Indra assumed a name for fame (middle), not naming a child. Faustos p.335 'դնել անուն դաստակերտին' verified: naming a town. The Gk/Ved/Arm 'put a name' formula is real (cognate noun + cognate verb), but the Norse anchor uses the renewed verb gefa, matching Latin 'nomen dare', German 'Namen geben' and Christian baptismal usage; so the Norse adds nothing diagnostic and could be derivative.

derivative_risk: medium (gefa nafn ~ Lat. nomen dare, baptismal naming)
known: *h1nómn̥ dʰeh1- 'put/establish a name' (Hitt. lāman dai-, Ved. nā́ma dhā-, Gk ὄνομα θέσθαι, Arm. anun dnel) is a well-known inherited collocation
